title: "stateMINT internals"
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use("styles/mint.mplstyle")
```

The emulator has to reproduce a trajectory rather than a number, predicting 157 fortnightly
windows in which what happens at one step depends on everything that came before it.

## The backbone

stateMINT is built on Mamba2, a state-space sequence model whose mechanism is a linear
recurrence. The model carries a hidden state, here of width `d_state` = 128, from one
timestep to the next, updating it with the current input and reading the output from it. It
is causal. The prediction at step $t$ depends only on the inputs up to $t$, which is the
right inductive bias for an epidemic evolving under an intervention. Nothing at year 5 may
depend on what the model is about to see at year 10.

The rest of the stack is short, and a linear projection lifts the 16 input features to
`d_model` = 256 before two Mamba2 blocks run over the sequence. Dropout is applied, and a
linear head reads one output per timestep.

```{python}
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

prevalence = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)
cases = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="cases", revision="v1.2.2",
)

prevalence.model_config
```

`output_dim` is 1 because each timestep predicts a single scalar, either a prevalence or a
case count. The two predictors are separately trained checkpoints of the same architecture.
They share no weights, no dropout rate and no scaler.

```{python}
print("cases dropout     :", cases.model_config["dropout"])
print("prevalence dropout:", prevalence.model_config["dropout"])
```

## The input tensor

`prepare_inputs` turns a list of covariate dicts into a `(B, 157, 16)` array. The sixteen
features per timestep fall into three groups.

| Columns | Group | What they are |
|---|---|---|
| 0–1 | Cyclical time | The sine and cosine of the day of year, giving the model a smooth, wrapped calendar rather than a sawtooth |
| 2–13 | Static covariates | The twelve covariates, standardised, broadcast across every timestep |
| 14–15 | Intervention | A post-campaign flag, and years since the campaign |

```{python}
import numpy as np

config = prevalence.preprocessing_config

covariates = dict(
    eir=31.96, dn0_use=0.311, dn0_future=0.457, Q0=0.85, phi_bednets=0.80,
    seasonal=0.0, routine=0.0, itn_use=0.70, irs_use=0.0,
    itn_future=0.70, irs_future=0.0, lsm=0.0,
)

X = prevalence.prepare_inputs([covariates])
print("shape:", X.shape, X.dtype)
print("static covariates:", config["static_covars"])
```

The static block is the same twelve numbers repeated 157 times, apart from the five
after-intervention covariates, which are zeroed before day 3285 (see
[Pipeline architecture](architecture.qmd)). The only columns that genuinely vary with time are the four at
either end.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The four time-varying features of the input tensor. The dashed rule marks the campaign at day 3285."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Left: sine and cosine of the day of year, oscillating over six years. Right: a post-campaign step from 0 to 1 at year 0, and a years-since-campaign ramp rising linearly from 0 to about 3."
abs_t = np.arange(
    config["model_start_day"],
    config["model_start_day"] + config["window_size"] * config["n_steps"],
    config["window_size"],
)
years = (abs_t - config["intervention_day"]) / 365

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3.4))

axes[0].plot(years, X[0, :, 0], label="sin(day of year)")
axes[0].plot(years, X[0, :, 1], label="cos(day of year)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("cyclical time")

axes[1].plot(years, X[0, :, 14], label="post-campaign flag")
axes[1].plot(years, X[0, :, 15], label="years since campaign")
axes[1].set_ylabel("intervention features")

for ax in axes:
    ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=1, alpha=0.7)
    ax.set_xlabel("years from campaign")
    ax.legend()

plt.show()
```

The cyclical pair is what allows `seasonal` to have an effect, because it gives the
recurrence a phase for the seasonal amplitude to attach to. The intervention pair tells the
model both *that* the campaign has happened and *how long ago*, so waning can be learned as
a function of time since deployment rather than of absolute date.

## Standardisation

The twelve static covariates are on very different scales, with EIR running into the
hundreds and coverages sitting in [0, 1]. They are standardised before the input projection.
The scaler is not a fitted object shipped as a pickle. It is two lists of plain JSON in
`preprocessing_config`, `scaler_mean` and `scaler_scale`, from which a `StandardScaler` is
rebuilt at load. Each covariate is transformed as $(x - \mu) / s$.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

pd.DataFrame({
    "covariate": config["static_covars"],
    "scaler_mean": config["scaler_mean"],
    "scaler_scale": config["scaler_scale"],
})
```

These are the means and standard deviations of the training library, so they also describe
the space the emulator has seen. An EIR of 400 is nearly 3.3 standard deviations from the
training mean. The model will return a value there, but it is not a value to rely on.

The masked zeros are masked in raw units and standardised afterwards, so a pre-campaign
`itn_future` appears in the tensor as $(0 - \mu) / s$, not as 0.

## Target transforms

Neither target is learned on its natural scale, since prevalence is a proportion and is
learned in **logit** space. Cases are counts with a long right tail, and are learned in
**log1p** space. `predict` inverts the transform for you (a sigmoid for prevalence, `expm1`
for cases) unless you ask for the model's own space with `transformed=True`.

```{python}
z = prevalence.predict([covariates], transformed=True)
y = prevalence.predict([covariates])

print("logit space:", z.min().round(3), "to", z.max().round(3))
print("prevalence :", y.min().round(3), "to", y.max().round(3))
print("sigmoid(z) == y:", np.allclose(1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)), y, atol=1e-6))
```

```{python}
z_cases = cases.predict([covariates], transformed=True)
y_cases = cases.predict([covariates])

print("expm1(z) == y   :", np.allclose(np.expm1(z_cases), y_cases, rtol=1e-5, atol=1e-4))
print("smallest log1p  :", float(z_cases.min()))
print("smallest cases  :", float(y_cases.min()))
```

The two transforms differ at the floor, because a sigmoid cannot leave [0, 1] whereas
`expm1` is not bounded below. Prevalence is bounded by construction. When the head's log1p
output falls below zero, as it can in a low-burden setting after an effective campaign,
`expm1` of it is negative, and `predict` returns a case count slightly below zero. This is
why `run_scenarios` applies `np.maximum(..., 0.0)` to the case series, and why its `cases`
column is floored where a bare `predict` is not.

## The artefact

Weights live on Hugging Face at `dide-ic/stateMINT`, one folder per predictor.

```
dide-ic/stateMINT
├── prevalence/
│   ├── checkpoint/                # Orbax
│   ├── model_config.json
│   └── preprocessing_config.json
└── cases/
    ├── checkpoint/
    ├── model_config.json
    └── preprocessing_config.json
```

`from_pretrained` downloads only the subfolder for the predictor you asked for, restores the
Orbax checkpoint into a `Mamba2Regressor` built from `model_config.json`, rebuilds the
scaler from `preprocessing_config.json`, and hands back a `ModelArtifact` holding all four.
The two config files are the contract between training and inference. `prepare_inputs`
reconstructs the timestep grid, the masking and the scaling from them, so inference
preprocessing cannot drift from what the model was trained on.
